findings.title: Device limit enforcement has a TOCTOU race that allows exceeding the configured limit
findings.body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the device count is checked with CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement is executed in a different database session. There is no transaction, lock, or atomic conditional insert guarding the limit, so concurrent requests can all observe count < limit and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so a race that lets an attacker create unbounded device rows defeats its purpose. The check-then-act should be made atomic (e.g., a single conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with an appropriate lock/unique constraint strategy), or the limit must be enforced with a DB-level guarantee.

findings.title: When the device limit is reached, existing devices are silently blocked from updating, breaking legitimate returning devices
findings.body: When count >= deviceLimit, CreateOrUpdateDevice calls updateDevice, which only UPDATEs a row if that device_id already exists AND its updated_at is within the expiration window. If the limit is reached and a returning device's row has expired (older than anonymousDeviceExpiration) or was deleted, rowsAffected == 0 and the function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The consequence is that once the limit is full, legitimate returning devices whose rows have aged out can never refresh their updated_at, so they are permanently rejected instead of replacing an expired row. The intended behavior for a limit is presumably to allow updates to existing (non-expired) devices and reject only genuinely new devices; expired rows should be evicted/replaced rather than causing a hard failure for the returning device.

The device limit is meant to bound device-tracking rows, not to disable anonymous authentication. The correct behavior is to log/metric the limit-reached condition and still return the anonymous identity (as was done for other TagDevice errors), so anonymous access keeps working while new device rows are refused.

Since TagDevice is invoked on anonymous requests (previously in a background goroutine, now synchronously), this adds a full table scan/count over the anon_device table to each request. findings.title: New device_limit setting has no validation and no documentation of its semantics (0 = unlimited)
findings.body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0). There is no validation that rejects negative values, and the semantics of 0 (unlimited, since the check is deviceLimit > 0) are not documented in the config. A negative value would silently behave as unlimited (because of the > 0 guard), which is likely not what an operator intends. The setting should either validate the value (reject negatives) or document the 0/negative behavior, and the new [auth.anonymous] device_limit option should be documented in the configuration docs.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as 'number | undefined' but backend always serializes an int64 (0 when unset)

The frontend type 'number | undefined' implies the field may be absent, but it will in practice always be present as a number; consumers checking for undefined will never see it. The type should be 'number' to match the actual wire contract, or the backend should use a pointer with omitempty if absence is meaningful.
